subtype: Plans and packages compared with a bad option in the mix [Receiver]
passage: Pema, you asked why I took so long choosing the new internet plan. So, it was Diwali week, the house was full of guests, and the old connection kept dropping. The company had three plans. Basic was slow and cheap. Then there was a middle plan that cost almost as much as the top one but was barely faster than basic. And the top one looked amazing next to it. I nearly clicked it right away. Then I stopped. Why would anyone ever choose that middle plan? It felt like it was there only to make the top one shine. So I covered it with my thumb and asked: what do I actually use? Two phones and a laptop for work calls. Basic plus a bit, really. So I, Devika, went with the cheaper one. It's been fine.

qa.q: How many phones does Devika's household use on the internet plan?
qa.a: Two phones and a laptop for work calls.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when first seeing the top plan?
qa.a: Devika felt tempted and impressed, nearly clicking it because it looked amazing next to the odd middle plan.

qa.q: What did Devika do to avoid being steered by the middle plan?
qa.a: Devika covered it with a thumb and asked what the household actually uses, then chose based on that.

qa.q: How might the internet company see the middle plan?
qa.a: The company may see it as a tool to make the top plan look like better value.

grounding: Shows an adult noticing an oddly poor plan that makes another look excellent, and pausing to ask what they really need.

passage: In a Dublin phone shop, Liam stared at the three offers on the screen. His friend Felix pointed at the most expensive. "That's the deal. Look, the middle one's nearly the same price for half the data." Liam nodded, then did something odd. He put his hand over the middle option. "Nobody would pick that one. It's just there to push us." He took out his phone notes. He had written his list the night before: calls to his mum in Poland, maps, some music, and a budget he'd set. He compared the cheap plan and the expensive one to that list, not to each other. "I don't stream on the bus. The cheap one covers it." Felix laughed. "You came prepared." "I've been caught before," Liam said.

qa.q: Who does Liam call on his phone?
qa.a: His mum in Poland.

qa.q: How does Liam seem to feel in the shop?
qa.a: He seems calm and in control, confident because he prepared his list in advance.

qa.q: What steps did Liam use to decide?
qa.a: He covered the option nobody would pick and compared the rest against his written list and budget.

qa.q: How does Felix see the offers at first?
qa.a: Felix is drawn to the expensive one because the middle option makes it look like a great deal.

grounding: Illustrates a buyer covering up the decoy option and deciding with a written list against his own needs.

passage: "I am the doctor!" Alka announced, pulling on Papa's old sweater like a coat. It was a cold winter morning, and the game had started after breakfast. "You're sick, Jasleen. Lie down." Jasleen lay on the rug. Alka listened with a spoon. After a while, Jasleen sat up. "Can we play shop now?" "No. I'm the doctor." "But this is boring." Alka frowned. It was boring. "I said I'm the doctor," she said firmly. "Doctors can't just stop." Jasleen sighed. "Can the doctor go to the shop?" Alka thought hard. "Okay. The doctor goes shopping."

qa.q: What did Alka use to listen to Jasleen?
qa.a: A spoon.

qa.q: Why did Alka refuse to change the game even though it was boring?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and stubborn about going back on what she had announced; being the doctor felt like a promise she had to keep.

qa.q: What clever idea helped the game move on?
qa.a: Jasleen asked if the doctor could go to the shop, letting Alka keep her word while changing the game.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel lying on the rug?
qa.a: Jasleen feels bored and restless, wanting a new game.

grounding: Shows a young child sticking to the role she announced even after the game stops being fun.

passage: In January, before the Republic Day sports meet, I did something big. In front of the whole class, I said, "I'm going to win the 200 metres." Everyone went "Ooooh." Ritu said, "Big talk, Jagdish." After that, I couldn't take it back. It was so cold in the mornings that my breath made clouds, but I went to the ground every day at six. Once I wanted to stay in my blanket, and then I thought of everyone hearing me say it. I got up. I didn't want to be the boy who said and didn't do. On race day, I came second. Ritu came first! But I ran my best time ever, and I think saying it out loud is why.

qa.q: What race did Jagdish say he would win?
qa.a: The 200 metres.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish get out of his blanket on the cold morning?
qa.a: He felt that he had to match his words, worried about being the boy who said something and didn't do it.

qa.q: How could Jagdish use this public-promise trick again, wisely?
qa.a: He could tell others about a goal he really wants, so the promise pushes him, while remembering that doing his best counts even if he doesn't win.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel after winning the race?
qa.a: Ritu probably felt happy and proud, and maybe amused after teasing Jagdish's big talk.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who announced he would win a race training harder so his actions match his word.

subtype: Stuck in a choice already paid for [Actor]
passage: Stockholm's winter was at its darkest, and Oskar was walking to his accounting evening class again. He hated it. He'd hated it since October. But he had paid for the full year, and he'd told his whole family, and his friend Diego, that he was going to be an accountant. At the class, he stared at spreadsheets and daydreamed about the carpentry workshop he passed every morning. "Why don't you just stop?" Diego asked over coffee. "I've done five months. And everyone knows." "So?" "So quitting means I was wrong." Diego shrugged. "You were wrong. So what?" Oskar felt a flash of annoyance. Walking home in the snow, he resented the course, the fee, and most of all himself for starting it.

qa.q: Where does Oskar walk past every morning?
qa.a: The carpentry workshop.

qa.q: What is Oskar feeling as he walks home in the snow?
qa.a: He feels resentful toward the course, the fee and himself, and stuck because quitting would mean admitting he was wrong.

qa.q: What question could help Oskar decide about the course?
qa.a: He could ask: knowing what I know now, would I sign up today? If not, the months already spent shouldn't decide the rest.

qa.q: How does Diego see Oskar's reason for staying?
qa.a: Diego sees it as unimportant; being wrong once is normal and shouldn't keep Oskar in a course he hates.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying in a disliked course because time and fees are spent and friends were told.

passage: Supervisor's note, quarterly review. Kiran had committed, in front of the whole team in January, to leading the new warehouse app. Last week Kiran came to me and said, plainly, "I want to change my decision. I agreed before we knew the vendor would drop support. With what we know now, a paper-and-scanner system is better for us." There was no drama and no long excuses. Kiran then explained the change to the team in five minutes, including what had been wrong in the earlier plan. Neelam, who'd been worried about losing face for the team, said afterwards that it made her respect Kiran more. What I did next: I asked Kiran to write a short note on how we decide big changes.

qa.q: What did Kiran commit to leading in January?
qa.a: The new warehouse app.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel after Kiran explained the change?
qa.a: Neelam went from worried about losing face to respecting Kiran more.

qa.q: What made Kiran's change of course graceful?
qa.a: Kiran accepted the old decision was made with less information and explained the change plainly without drama or excuses.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling when coming to the supervisor?
qa.a: Kiran may have felt a little nervous but clear-headed and confident about the new information.

grounding: Illustrates an adult changing an earlier public decision gracefully by explaining it plainly in light of new information.

subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]
passage: It was the first week of the Ramzan holidays, and cousin Farida was in charge while the aunties cooked for iftar. "Farida Didi, can I play the phone game for just five minutes?" asked Ankita. "Okay, five." Five minutes later: "Just five more? I'm on a hard level." "Fine." Then: "Can I finish this world? It's almost done." Farida looked up from her book. Ankita was curled on the sofa, eyes glued to the screen. "Didi, just till the azaan? Then I'll stop." Farida nodded without thinking. When the azaan finally sounded, she looked at the clock and blinked. Two hours! "Ankita! How did five minutes become two hours?" Ankita grinned sheepishly. "You kept saying yes."

qa.q: How long did Ankita first ask to play?
qa.a: Just five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Ankita grin sheepishly at the end?
qa.a: She felt a bit guilty and amused, knowing she had turned each small yes into a bigger one on purpose.

qa.q: What could Farida do next time Ankita asks for "just five more"?
qa.a: She could set a clear total at the start and stick to it, asking herself whether she'd agree to the whole evening if asked first.

qa.q: How does Farida feel when she sees the clock?
qa.a: Farida is surprised and a bit annoyed at herself, realising small yeses added up to two hours.

grounding: Shows a child turning a small request into a bigger one step by step, each yes making the next seem natural.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage: In the winter exam season, I, Reena, signed an online pledge to save the lake near our school. One click, my name, done. I felt good. A week later, the group messaged: "Thanks for pledging! Can you share the poster on your status?" Sure, easy. Then: "Can you volunteer every Sunday for two months?" I had exams. I wanted to say no. But I kept thinking, I said I care about the lake. Saying no now would make me a fake. My friend Pema noticed me stressing. "You can care about the lake and still say no to Sundays," she said. I wrote back that I could help one Sunday after exams. I felt guilty for a day. Then I felt fine.

qa.q: What did Reena sign an online pledge for?
qa.a: To save the lake near the school.

qa.q: Why did Reena feel she couldn't say no to volunteering every Sunday?
qa.a: Reena felt guilty and torn, because refusing seemed to contradict the care for the lake that the pledge had shown.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make, and why was it reasonable?
qa.a: Reena offered one Sunday after exams, which fit real priorities while still supporting the cause.

qa.q: How does Pema see Reena's dilemma?
qa.a: Pema sees that caring about the lake and saying no to Sundays are not in conflict.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who, after a tiny pledge, finds a larger follow-up hard to refuse because saying no feels inconsistent.

subtype: Refusing a huge favour, then feeling bound by a smaller one [Receiver]
passage: It was the week before Diwali, and the hostel was emptying out. Zainab knocked on my door. "Tenzin, can I borrow your scooter for the whole holiday? I'll bring it back after." Ten days, a long road trip. I said no; I needed it. She looked crushed. "Okay, okay. Then could you at least drop me at the station at five tomorrow morning?" And I heard myself say yes before I'd even thought. Five a.m.! I hate early mornings. Later, lying awake, I realised: she'd dropped the big ask, and I felt I owed her a yes. Like she'd given something up, so it was my turn. I did drop her. I didn't mind, really. But next time, I'll ask myself if I'd say yes to the small thing on its own.

qa.q: What time did Zainab need to be dropped at the station?
qa.a: At five the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin say yes to the early-morning drop so quickly?
qa.a: Tenzin felt guilty after refusing the scooter, as if Zainab had given something up and it was now Tenzin's turn to agree.

qa.q: What will Tenzin ask next time, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Whether the smaller request would be a yes on its own, so the first refusal doesn't push Tenzin into agreeing.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt about the lift?
qa.a: Zainab likely felt relieved and grateful, maybe without noticing the pressure her second ask created.

grounding: Shows a young adult who, after refusing a big favour, feels bound to accept a smaller compromise.

subtype: Asking whether it would be a yes as a first request [Response]
passage: In the call centre's break room, Tanuja caught Nazia by the coffee machine. "Could you cover my whole weekend shift? Both days? My cousin's engagement." Nazia shook her head. "I can't, I've got my own plans." "Oh. Then just Sunday morning? Only four hours." Nazia felt the familiar pull to say yes. Tanuja had backed down; it felt rude not to meet her halfway. But she paused. Would I say yes if she'd only asked for Sunday morning in the first place? She thought about her own Sunday: her mother's visit, finally. "Honestly, no. I'm sorry, Tanuja. I hope you find someone. Try asking Rehan, he wanted extra hours." Tanuja nodded. Nazia walked back to her desk, surprised by how light she felt.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja need the weekend off?
qa.a: Her cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when Tanuja asked for just Sunday morning?
qa.a: She felt the familiar pull of guilt to agree, as if refusing again would be rude after Tanuja backed down.

qa.q: What question helped Nazia decide, and what did she do?
qa.a: She asked whether she'd agree to Sunday morning as a first request, realised no, and declined kindly while suggesting Rehan.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel after Nazia's second no?
qa.a: Tanuja may feel disappointed but helped by the suggestion to ask Rehan.

grounding: Illustrates an adult asking whether a smaller follow-up request would be a yes on its own, and feeling free to decline.
